set.approach: From the Molas trailhead the trail drops about 1,700 feet over roughly four miles to the Animas River and crosses a bridge. Climb along the Colorado Trail for about 1.5 miles to the beaver ponds, then follow the steep, well-worn trail about two miles up into Vestal Basin, where a few fallen trees lie between roughly 10,000 and 10,300 feet. Many parties camp in the basin and climb from there; the climbing starts at the base of the north face above the basin.
set.descent_text: Do not take the first trail leading off the summit; it is loose, with kitty-litter ledges and 15-foot Class 3 downclimbs. Instead, from the back of the subsummit, descend a loose gully that stays at Class 3 or easier, cross the rib to your right where cairns mark a gap in it, then reach the saddle trail and the moraines that lead back to the basin camp.
hazards: Loose scree and kitty litter on the wrong descent trail
Exposed Class 3 downclimbs off the summit
Easy fifth-class upper ridge with a steep slab that is best bypassed
Long approach with a 1,700-foot climb back out at the end of the day

review.notes: Approach and descent come from one detailed report of the route; the approach is written as facts of the trail, not as a report. Skipped season (no page stated one). Gain/distance not in fill.

set.overview: A Class 2 walk up the south slope of Clinton Peak in the Mosquito Range, starting from the Montgomery Reservoir road south of Hoosier Pass. The route crosses a basin of water, mud and willows, then climbs tundra and talus with little exposure and easy route-finding. It is often done with the neighboring McNamee and Traver, which are reached along the ridge.
set.approach: From Colorado 9 just south of Hoosier Pass, turn west on County Road 4 and follow it to the west end of Montgomery Reservoir, where passenger cars park near 10,970 feet. Past that point the road is a rough four-wheel-drive track with rock slabs, deep mud and water crossings, so it is usually walked. Follow the Middle Fork of the South Platte upstream toward Wheeler Lake, then go up into the basin below Clinton, McNamee and Traver, and climb the south slope from there.
set.descent_text: Return the way you came: come down the south slope into the basin, cross the central stream, and walk the track out past Wheeler Lake to the reservoir. Descending the ridge toward McNamee and Traver is the alternative if linking peaks.
hazards: Dense willows, water and mud on the road and in the basin
Loose talus and rubble on the slopes
Rough four-wheel-drive road with rock slabs and a steep step
Snow in the basin early in the season can call for an ice axe

review.notes: Source pages describe the Traver-McNamee-Clinton combination (about 10-12.8 mi, 3,200-3,300 ft), not the south slope alone, so distance left out. Skipped season. Descent for Clinton alone is inferred as retracing the climb.

set.approach: About 7 miles east of Moab on River Road, park at a small pullout on the river side, just past a large boulder with calcite on one side. Walk back toward Moab on the road to a trail marked by a metal post; the walk takes about 20 minutes to the west face. The route is on the east side, so first climb a short 5.7 approach pitch up a loose corner to a belay anchor in the south-side notch, then walk along the base of the northeast face to the chalked chimney.
set.descent_text: No anchors exist on the summit, so reverse the mantle onto the summit block and downclimb to the fixed anchors. Then either rappel the route with two ropes, walk to the approach-pitch anchors and rappel to your packs, or use a single 70 m rope down the northeast side, a short rappel to a ledge and a long one to the back of the spire.
hazards: Approach pitch is run-out and loose
No summit anchor; the overhanging summit block must be mantled and reversed
Wet sandstone is weak: do not climb in or just after rain
Heat in summer and spring raptor closures

review.notes: Gain/distance skipped. Rappel counts left out.

set.approach: Drive the signed Davis Canyon road, which turns to high-clearance four-wheel-drive track within a short distance, and park where a track bends toward the foot of the talus cone; the tower stands west of the road. Do not take the southern line that heads into scrambling over the white rim. Head instead for a gap in the rim further north, follow the rim along until you are below the east face, and finish up a passable trail over the last hump. Liquid Sky and the neighbouring roof crack are visible above as you arrive.
set.descent_text: From the summit, rappel south into the chimney and notch above the big roof, where an old bolt ladder sits; inspect it before trusting it. From the notch, rappel on three bolts of doubtful quality along the formation's west side to the ground, so back up or replace worn anchors if you can.
hazards: Squeeze chimney through a roof that is strongly dependent on body size and can stop a larger climber
Rappel bolts on the west side of the tower and the old bolt ladder in the notch are of doubtful quality
Long sections of offwidth and squeeze climbing that are strenuous and awkward to protect
Sandstone is fragile when wet and holds can break, so avoid climbing during or just after rain

review.notes: Season, gain, distance skipped: no page opened states them. Descent is the tower's normal descent as the area page describes it, not specific to this line.

set.approach: Park at the lot where the Courthouse Wash trail begins, on its north end. Walk the trail a few minutes until you are level with Argon Tower, then follow intermittent climbers' trails around the north end of the tower. These lead past the lower part of the tower to a bench on its west side, ten to fifteen minutes from the lot.
set.descent_text: Rappel the west face from the top of the fourth pitch. Two 60 m ropes may reach the ground in one rappel, but be ready to stop at a midway anchor and rappel again if you cannot see the ground.
hazards: Sandy, soft rock; a placed cam can be hard to remove
Poorly protected and loose holds on the upper corner pitch
Finish relies on a bolt ladder that is climbed on aid
Sandstone is fragile when wet, so avoid climbing during or after rain

review.notes: Season, gain, distance skipped. Pitch count on the route page is five whereas the database overview says four; I avoided giving a count.

set.overview: Mokelumne Peak is the high point of the northern Mokelumne Wilderness, a rounded summit reached from the Tanglefoot trailhead by a trail and a short cross-country stretch. The route dips into Tanglefoot Canyon, leaves the trail in open forest, then climbs through brush to a saddle and follows an easy ridge to the top. It is class 2, and the main task is navigation through forest and manzanita.
set.approach: Reach the Tanglefoot trailhead by dirt roads from Bear River Reservoir; the roads are confusing and a GPS helps. Hike the trail through Tanglefoot Canyon, down one side and up the other, passing a small lake. Where the forest opens up, leave the trail, pass south of the bump at 8,628 ft, and head up to the saddle that joins that bump to Mokelumne Peak, working around the brush. A grassy watercourse is one way up to the saddle, and the ridge from there to the summit is easy.
hazards: Dense forest with few landmarks makes it hard to find where to leave the trail
Thick manzanita brush on the climb to the saddle
Little water: one spring on the climb out of Tanglefoot Canyon

evidence.fact: about 13 miles round trip; halved (6.5 mi)

review.notes: Assumes the row's standard route is the Tanglefoot line. Descent not stated; season not stated (late September and early August reports).
